items.title: Ouagadougou : Des experts outillent les marketeurs à l’Intelligence artificielle pour doper la performance
items.description: Une masterclass co-animée par le Dr Sambo Kalifa Sankara et Bili Edouard Tieno a réuni praticiens et dirigeants autour de cas concrets d’application de l’IA, le jeudi 30 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou. L’enjeu : concilier gain de productivité, retour sur investissement et protection du patrimoine informationnel dans un contexte africain. Comment l’intelligence artificielle peut-elle servir concrètement la fonction marketing en Afrique, sans se substituer au jugement humain ni exposer les données stratégiques des entreprises ? C’est la question qui a structuré la masterclass intitulée « L’intelligence artificielle appliquée au marketing : Booster la performance marketing dans un contexte africain », co-animée par le Dr Sambo Kalifa Sankara, expert en intelligence artificielle, et Bili Edouard Tieno, expert en stratégie marketing. Dr Sankara présentant un panorama d’outils, généralistes ou spécifiquement dédiés au marketing Devant un auditoire composé de professionnels et de dirigeants, les deux intervenants ont déroulé une approche résolument opérationnelle. « Ce qui a été donné aux différents participants, c’est les bases de l’IA appliquées au marketing sur des cas concrets », a expliqué le Dr Sankara. Cinq cas précis ont été disséqués pour démontrer que l’IA permet de traiter plus rapidement des problématiques complexes et, surtout, de révéler « ce qui n’est pas visible à l’œil nu ». Un panorama d’outils, généralistes ou spécifiquement dédiés au marketing, a été présenté. Mais l’expert en IA a tenu à poser un préalable méthodologique. « On peut avoir tous les outils du marché, si vous n’avez pas bien défini votre besoin, vos outils ne vous servent absolument à rien », a-t-il prévenu. Le procès, a insisté Dr Sankara, consiste d’abord à penser le besoin, avant de choisir la technologie. Pour Bili Edouard Tieno, l’appropriation de l’IA par les métiers du marketing et du développement commercial n’est plus une option. « Aujourd’hui, c’est inéluctable. La fonction marketing au sein des organisations est le moteur de la pérennité, de la croissance et du développement des entités », a-t-il affirmé. L’IA doit être comprise comme « une prolongation de leur capacité, de leur potentiel », au service de l’efficience et de l’efficacité. Face à un environnement économique en mutation, M. Tieno a lancé un appel aux praticiens à se mettre à niveau pour assurer le succès des organisations et impacter positivement l’environnement immédiat. « On n’arrête pas le développement. Il faut composer avec le développement », a-t-il souligné. Pour Bili Edouard Tieno, l’appropriation de l’IA par les métiers du marketing et du développement commercial n’est plus une option Les témoignages recueillis à l’issue de la session confirment l’acuité des attentes. Joël Ki, directeur général de Wave Mobile Money au Burkina Faso, retient deux enseignements majeurs. « Côté AI, j’ai vraiment appris qu’il y a toute cette notion de sécurité, de confidentialité, de données, en tout cas de sécurisation de nos données, c’est super important », a-t-il confié. Sur le volet marketing, M. Ki a souligné la possibilité d’aller « très vite » et de « faire bien » en cumulant les fonctions marketing et l’intelligence artificielle. Mais son attention a été particulièrement captée par l’exigence de retour sur investissement. « Si on peut dépenser moins et générer beaucoup plus, c’est encore mieux avec l’AI », a-t-il fait savoir. Cette question de la maîtrise des données et du savoir-faire irrigue également les préoccupations de Mahamadi Rouamba, directeur général de TICAnalyse. Sans contester l’apport de l’IA, il invite à la prudence. « On n’a pas encore trouvé de meilleur outil de production que cela. Mais il faut faire très attention parce que c’est dans cette capacité également que l’on risque, en fait, de perdre beaucoup en termes de savoir-faire, en termes d’informations qui peuvent constituer un capital pour une entreprise », a-t-il conclu. items.title: Israël : après des élections sans majorité, le spectre d’une nouvelle crise politique
items.description: Trois jours apres les elections legislatives du 27 octobre, Israel se retrouve dans une impasse politique. Le depouillement confirme l'avance de Benjamin Netanyahou, mais aucun des deux grands blocs ne dispose des 61 sieges necessaires pour gouverner. Le Premier ministre sortant conserve une coalition de 53 deputes, contre 48 pour l'opposition menee par Gadi Eisenkot, ancien chef d'etat-major. Entre les deux, les partis arabes realisent une percee historique avec 19 elus, devenant les arbitres potentiels du prochain gouvernement. La suite se jouera entre les mains du president Isaac Herzog. Apres la transmission officielle des resultats, prevue le 4 novembre, il consultera les differentes formations avant de designer le depute qu'il estime le mieux place pour constituer une majorite. Celui-ci disposera de 28 jours, avec une prolongation possible de 14 jours, pour former son gouvernement. En cas d'echec, d'autres candidats pourront tenter leur chance. Vers une crise politique Plusieurs scenarios se dessinent. Netanyahou pourrait tenter de convaincre une partie de l'opposition de rejoindre un gouvernement d'union nationale. Une alliance avec Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett et Avigdor Liberman lui offrirait une majorite, mais supposerait de rompre avec certains de ses allies religieux et d'extreme droite. Surtout, ses adversaires ont jusqu'ici refuse de gouverner sous son autorite. L'ancien chef d'etat-major pourrait, de son cote, chercher a former un gouvernement minoritaire beneficiant du soutien exterieur des partis arabes. L'ensemble reunirait theoriquement 67 deputes, mais Bennett et Liberman rejettent l'idee. Reuters En attendant, le chef du Likoud restera Premier ministre par interim, meme sans majorite parlementaire. Si aucune des negociations n'aboutit, de nouvelles elections seraient envisageables en 2027, rappelant l'instabilite qui avait conduit Israel a voter cinq fois entre 2019 et 2022. Faute de compromis, le pays risque donc de prolonger une crise dont les consequences depassent ses frontieres, au moment ou les dossiers de Gaza, du Liban et de l'Iran demeurent particulierement sensibles.

items.title: CAN: la CAF fait marche arrière et rétablit le rythme biennal
items.description: La Coupe d’Afrique des Nations (CAN) retrouvera son rythme habituel de deux ans. Réuni le jeudi 29 octobre 2026, le Comité exécutif de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF) a décidé à l’unanimité de revenir sur la réforme qui prévoyait une organisation tous les quatre ans. Une décision que son président, Patrice Motsepe, justifie par la défense des intérêts du football africain et les enjeux financiers liés à la future Ligue des Nations. C’est un changement de cap pour le football continental. La CAF a officiellement renoncé à son projet de faire disputer la CAN tous les quatre ans. À l’issue de sa réunion du jeudi 29 octobre 2026, son Comité exécutif a rétabli la périodicité biennale de la compétition, mettant ainsi fin à une réforme annoncée l’année précédente. Cette révision avait été évoquée par le président de l'instance, Patrice Motsepe, lors de la Conférence stratégique de la CAF, organisée au Cap-Vert du 7 au 9 octobre 2026. À cette occasion, le dirigeant sud-africain avait annoncé que le Comité exécutif réexaminerait la décision de passer à un cycle quadriennal. Dans un communiqué publié sur son site officiel, la CAF explique que ce réexamen s'appuie notamment sur les incertitudes entourant la mise en place de la nouvelle Ligue des Nations africaine. Cette compétition, envisagée comme un rendez-vous biennal devant remplacer l'actuelle CAN, nécessiterait plusieurs années avant de générer des ressources financières suffisamment importantes pour soutenir le développement du football africain. Patrice Motsepe a défendu le bien-fondé de cette nouvelle orientation. «La décision du Comité exécutif de la CAF de rétablir l’organisation de la CAN tous les deux ans vise à faire progresser, à protéger et à promouvoir les intérêts du football africain et des 54 Associations Membres de la CAF, ainsi que ceux des joueurs africains évoluant dans des clubs en dehors du continent», a-t-il déclaré. Le président de la CAF a également insisté sur les limites financières du projet de Ligue des Nations. «Nous étions également préoccupés par le nombre d’années nécessaires avant que la nouvelle compétition panafricaine proposée, la Ligue des Nations, conçue pour être identique à l’actuelle CAN et se disputer tous les deux ans, puisse apporter les contributions financières substantielles et les retombées nécessaires au développement du football africain, afin de rendre les compétitions de la CAF compétitives à l’échelle mondiale et financièrement autonomes», a-t-il expliqué. Concernant le calendrier, la prochaine édition de la CAN est prévue en 2027 au Kenya, en Tanzanie et en Ouganda. Les éditions suivantes se tiendront en 2028, 2031 et 2033. «La prochaine édition de la TotalEnergies CAF Coupe d’Afrique des Nations aura lieu en 2027 au Kenya, en Tanzanie et en Ouganda, et je suis convaincu qu’elle connaîtra un grand succès», a assuré Patrice Motsepe. Le calendrier continental devra toutefois tenir compte de celui des grandes compétitions internationales. La Coupe du monde de la FIFA étant programmée en 2030, les phases finales de la CAN et des autres compétitions de sélections nationales des confédérations pourraient ne pas se tenir durant cette année-là, conformément à la tradition de la FIFA. Pour le patron de l'instance dirigeante du football africain, cette décision constitue une orientation favorable à l'avenir du ballon rond sur le continent. «La décision du Comité exécutif de la CAF sert au mieux les intérêts du football africain et des 54 Associations Membres de la CAF. Elle contribuera également de manière significative au développement et à la croissance du football en Afrique», a-t-il conclu. En rétablissant la CAN tous les deux ans, la CAF privilégie ainsi la continuité de sa compétition phare et entend préserver les intérêts sportifs et économiques du football africain. Un retour à l'ancien rythme qui redessine déjà le calendrier des grandes échéances continentales pour les prochaines années. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article CAN: la CAF fait marche arrière et rétablit le rythme biennal est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Ghana Medical Trust Fund courts US partners to expand cancer care
items.description: The Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF) is seeking partnerships with American hospitals, investors and philanthropists to expand cancer treatment and other specialist healthcare services in Ghana. The Fund’s Administrator, Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, made the appeal at the Ghana-Tennessee Business and Investor Roundtable in Nashville, Tennessee. She said partnerships could help close gaps in diagnostics, treatment, specialist training, and hospital infrastructure while easing patients’ financial burden. “For many families, a diagnosis is difficult enough. But the next question is often even more frightening: how are we going to afford the treatment, and where can we access this care?” she said. Ms Darko-Opoku said the Fund had enrolled more than 800 patients for treatment under its services package. It covers 13 common cancers, neurosurgical conditions, cardiovascular diseases and kidney diseases. Outlining the Fund’s work, she said it had reconstructed the cardiac catheterisation laboratory at Korle Bu Teaching Hospital after a fire disrupted services. According to her, the facility has supported more than 160 procedures since it was commissioned, including 110 involving children. She said oncology centres were under construction at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital in Kumasi and Tamale Teaching Hospital. The Fund is also working with the KGL Group on a proposed $10 million diagnostic and imaging centre at Ridge Hospital. The project aims to improve access to MRI, CT scans, and mammography. Plans are also underway for an advanced comprehensive oncology centre at Korle Bu to ease pressure on existing facilities and reduce waiting times. Ms Darko-Opoku said the Fund was investing close to GH¢1 billion in medical equipment for major hospitals. These include dialysis machines, intensive care beds, oxygen concentrators and patient monitors. To address workforce shortages, the Fund is sponsoring the training of 100 specialist pharmacists and 100 specialist nurses. It is also supporting specialist medical training centres in six regions. She identified infrastructure, medical technology, specialist training, research and financial assistance for vulnerable patients as priority areas for US partnerships. The Fund is also exploring adding treatments such as kidney transplantation to its services package. Ms Darko-Opoku said government resources alone could not meet Ghana’s growing specialist healthcare needs. She urged American institutions and the Ghanaian diaspora to commit to specific projects with clear implementation plans and measurable outcomes. “We are open to partnerships that bring together investment, technical expertise and a shared commitment to results,” she said. Potential support could include diagnostic equipment, clinical exchanges, cancer care facilities, research funding and treatment assistance for patients who cannot afford care. “What we have achieved so far shows what is possible. With the right partnerships, we can do much more,” she said.

items.title: Ghanival 2026 to bring Brazilian carnival experience to Accra on December 12
items.description: Ghana is set to host a new cultural and entertainment event, Ghanival 2026, which will combine elements of Brazilian carnival with Ghanaian music, culture, fashion, food and dance. The event is scheduled for Saturday, December 12, at the University of Ghana Sports Complex, Legon, in Accra. Organisers say the festival will serve as an opening event for the December festivities while launching a broader cultural celebration towards Ghana’s 70th Independence anniversary in 2027. Ghanival is expected to feature live music, entertainment, carnival performances, fashion, food and other cultural activities, bringing together Ghanaians, members of the diaspora and international visitors. The initiative seeks to blend Brazil’s renowned carnival tradition with Ghana’s cultural identity to create an entertainment experience inspired by the two countries. The launch also comes ahead of the 2027 Rio Carnival, where one of Brazil’s leading samba schools, Acadêmicos do Grande Rio, is expected to showcase a theme exploring historical links between Brazil and Ghana. The school’s announced theme, “Sankofa Tabon – Os Retornados da Costa do Ouro e a Estrela Negra da Liberdade,” focuses on the history of the Tabon people, their return from Brazil to the Gold Coast and the historical connections between the two countries. Organisers say Ghanival will provide an opportunity to celebrate those cultural connections in Ghana, bringing together local and international audiences through music, dance and other creative expressions. Beyond the December 2026 event, the organisers intend to develop Ghanival into a larger cultural platform ahead of Ghana’s 70th Independence anniversary. The proposed 2027 celebration will focus on Ghana’s history, heritage, music, fashion, food, creative industries, tourism and entrepreneurship. Ghanival 2026 is expected to attract music lovers, families, young people, creatives, tourists and members of the diaspora as part of Accra’s December entertainment season.

items.title: A call for support and solidarity with ministers from Volta Region amid incessant attacks by NPP
items.description: The incessant attacks on Ministers from the Volta Region by the New Patriotic Party (NPP) and sections of the media perceived as sympathetic to it are increasingly worrying. In my view, we are witnessing a deliberate and unfortunate pattern of attempts to undermine the credibility, integrity, and contributions of some of the Volta Region’s finest political leaders. From Abla Dzifa Gomashie to Kwame Agbodza, and now Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, the recurring attacks raise legitimate questions about the motivations behind these campaigns. Political accountability and constructive criticism are essential ingredients of our democracy. However, there is a clear distinction between holding public officials accountable and engaging in sustained personal attacks and unsubstantiated allegations intended to damage their reputations and distract from their responsibilities. Our Ministers deserve to be assessed fairly on their performance, decisions and contributions to national development, rather than being subjected to what appears to be a coordinated campaign of political vilification. I call on the NDC in the Volta Region, particularly our vibrant Youth Wing, to stand firm in solidarity with our Ministers. We must remain vigilant, united and resolute in defending their integrity against unfounded allegations and politically motivated attacks, while continuing to uphold the principles of transparency and accountability. The Volta Region has contributed immensely to the NDC’s political fortunes and Ghana’s development. We must never allow partisan attacks to diminish the contributions of our distinguished representatives in government. We must stand together, speak with one voice and defend our own when they are unfairly targeted. An attack on the reputation of one of our leaders without credible justification deserves a collective, principled response. Julius Karl D. Fieve Deputy Volta Regional Youth Organiser Aspirant National Democratic Congress (NDC)

items.title: Disrupted LPG supply
items.description: THE petroleum minister’s explanation in the National Assembly that the recent closure of the Iran border has disrupted liquefied petroleum gas supplies and driven up prices identifies a major cause of the current crisis. The subsequent partial border reopening has failed to ease the shortage. While the closure may have triggered the present shortages and price hike, the problem recurs every winter. Pakistan produces only about a quarter of the LPG it needs. The rest is imported, mainly from Iran. The disruption of cross-border trade has therefore exposed the vulnerability of a market that depends heavily on external supplies. The Iran war has also complicated efforts to bring in more by sea. The minister says efforts are being made to increase seaborne supplies, but consumers have yet to see relief. The state must explain what additional volumes have been secured, and when they will arrive. Further, why were no contingency measures taken before the Iran border closure, especially when the authorities knew that the onset of winter would push up demand? The decision-makers owe an explanation to people suffering due to sudden shortages and price shock. That said, the current LPG supply disruption is only part of the wider story. LPG prices have historically surged as winter approaches, even without a major supply shock. This recurring pattern suggests that the crisis is not simply the result of border closure. Inadequate advance planning, weak market oversight and the failure to build reliable supply arrangements leave consumers exposed whenever demand rises or imports are interrupted. The consequences are particularly harsh for households without access to piped natural gas. Millions of families in northern Pakistan, remote and hilly areas, and parts of Punjab depend on LPG for cooking and, during colder months, heating. Low gas pressure and restricted supplies in connected areas also push more consumers towards cylinders, adding to demand. With the official price around Rs280 per kg and reported market rates reaching Rs500-800, an essential fuel has become unaffordable for many. Blaming the Iran border closure is but an attempt to cover up the ministry’s failure to do its basic duty: ensure adequate supplies ahead of the closure and enforce the official fuel price. Published in Dawn, October 30th, 2026

items.title: Mondial 2026 : la FIFA engrange près de 5 milliards de dollars grâce à la billetterie
items.description: La Coupe du monde 2026 aura été particulièrement lucrative pour la FIFA. Selon le média américain The Athletic, les ventes de billets et les prestations d’hospitalité devraient générer près de 5 milliards de dollars de recettes, soit cinq fois plus que lors du Mondial 2022 au Qatar. Une performance portée notamment par l’élargissement du tournoi à 48 équipes et une politique tarifaire sans précédent. La Coupe du monde 2026 a changé d’échelle, y compris sur le plan financier. Organisée aux États-Unis, au Canada et au Mexique, la compétition aurait permis à la FIFA de réaliser des recettes record grâce à la billetterie. Selon les informations de The Athletic, les ventes de billets et les forfaits d’hospitalité auraient rapporté près de 5 milliards de dollars, soit un montant cinq fois supérieur à celui enregistré lors de l’édition 2022 au Qatar. Cette progression s'explique notamment par le nouveau format de la compétition. Pour la première fois, 48 sélections ont participé au tournoi, contre 32 lors des précédentes éditions. Le nombre de rencontres est ainsi passé de 64 à 140, multipliant les possibilités de commercialisation des places et des prestations d'accueil. Au total, les recettes générées par cette édition pourraient atteindre 15 milliards de dollars, selon les estimations rapportées par le média américain. La billetterie et l'hospitalité représenteraient ainsi environ un tiers de ce montant. Des billets à des prix historiques Cette performance financière s'explique également par des tarifs particulièrement élevés. La Coupe du monde 2026 a proposé les billets les plus chers de l'histoire du tournoi. Pour assister à la finale opposant l'Espagne à l'Argentine, en juillet dernier, le prix d'entrée le plus bas aurait atteint 4 185 dollars, soit environ 3 500 euros. Un tarif près de sept fois supérieur à celui du billet le moins cher proposé pour la finale du Mondial 2022 au Qatar. Malgré ces prix, la demande est restée particulièrement forte. La FIFA a indiqué que 6,81 millions de supporters avaient assisté aux rencontres de cette édition, avec un taux de remplissage global de 99,7 %. Un chiffre qui témoigne de l'attractivité commerciale de la compétition, mais aussi de la capacité de la FIFA à tirer profit de l'élargissement du tournoi et de son organisation sur trois marchés majeurs. The post Mondial 2026 : la FIFA engrange près de 5 milliards de dollars grâce à la billetterie appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

JOJ Dakar 2026 : Volker Türk salue « une étape historique »
items.description: À la veille de l'ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ), le Haut-Commissaire des Nations Unies aux droits de l'homme salue une étape historique pour le continent africain et rappelle que le sport est un levier au service de la dignité et de l'égalité. Dans une vidéo diffusée avant le lancement de des JOJ akar2026, le Haut-Commissaire des Nations Unies aux droits de l'homme, Volker Türk, a adressé un message appuyé aux athlètes, aux fédérations et au monde sportif. Il y rappelle que le sport peut rassembler au-delà des frontières, combattre la discrimination et permettre à chaque jeune, quelles que soient ses origines, de participer, de compétir et de se sentir inclus. Une première olympique en Afrique Volker Türk s'est d'abord adressé aux participants de cette quatrième édition estivale des Jeux de la jeunesse : « Je salue les milliers de jeunes athlètes qui se rassembleront à Dakar au Sénégal au cours des prochaines semaines. Ils entrent dans l'histoire en participant à la toute première manifestation olympique organisée en Afrique. » Pour lui, cet événement dépasse le cadre sportif : « Le sport porte en lui une promesse de dignité et d'égalité pour tous et toutes, tout comme les droits humains. » Il en tire un principe : « Les grands événements sportifs devraient être accessibles à tous et à toutes et se dérouler partout. » Le Haut-Commissaire a rendu hommage à celles et ceux qui œuvrent à tenir cette promesse « dans l'esprit de la Charte Olympique et de la Déclaration universelle des droits de l'homme ». Il a aussi souligné ce que le parcours d'un athlète a de commun avec le combat pour les droits : « La réussite sportive repose sur la ténacité, le courage et la détermination à se dépasser, quelle que soit son origine. » Une génération face aux grands défis Le message s'est ensuite tourné vers les enjeux qui attendent cette génération : « Les jeunes athlètes d'aujourd'hui font partie d'une génération qui fait face déjà à certains des défis majeurs de notre époque : l'urgence climatique, le racisme et la discrimination, les discours de haine, les inégalités, les conflits et les incertitudes liées à l'intelligence artificielle. » Volker Türk a plaidé pour que les jeunes soient associés aux décisions : « Les jeunes réclament une place à la table des décisions et la possibilité de contribuer aux choix qui façonneront leur avenir. Tout comme le sport, les droits humains ont besoin de personnes engagées. » Le Haut-Commissaire a rappelé l'initiative qu'il a lancée plus tôt dans l'année : « J'ai lancé l'Alliance mondiale pour les droits humains au début de cette année pour amplifier les efforts de toutes les personnes partout dans le monde qui défendent les droits humains. » Il a conclu par une invitation directe au monde sportif : « J'espère que les jeunes, les athlètes, les fédérations et autres du monde du sport rejoindront notre Alliance. Ne restez pas sur la touche, entrez sur le terrain, battez-vous pour les droits, et je vous souhaite beaucoup de succès pour les Jeux. »

items.title: Human rights lawyer couple sentenced to 10 years’ prison in Pakistan
items.description: A Pakistani anti-terrorism court has sentenced human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari and her husband Hadi Ali Chattha to 10 years in prison, over an alleged security breach during a cricket tour in 2024. The couple were accused of removing road barriers and obstructing police officers in Islamabad – charges that both have denied. Mazari and Chattha were previously sentenced to up to 17 years in prison for social media posts criticising the military. Pakistan’s Supreme Court had suspended those sentences in August, but police re-arrested the couple before they could be released. They have been imprisoned in Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail for the past several months. This latest case concerns an incident on 25 October 2024, when England’s cricket team was touring Pakistan. Prosecutors accused Mazari and Chattha of removing barriers from a road designated for the team’s security convoy and obstructing police officers at Zero Point, a major cloverleaf road junction in Islamabad. They were each sentenced to 10 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Act, as well as additional one-year and two-year terms for obstructing and using force against public servants. All sentences will run concurrently. The court also fined each of them 200,000 Pakistani Rupees (£541:$723). In statements recorded during the trial, the couple described themselves as “prisoners of conscience” who had faced state persecution. “I am being punished for not only supporting my wife’s work and activism, but for choosing this path of resisting injustice as our life journey together,” Chatta said in his statement to Dawn News. The couple had earlier said that they were “being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression, and injustice”. Amnesty International has criticised the proceedings, saying the couple were denied an open and fair trial. “These convictions are an indictment of Pakistan’s justice system.” said Yasmine Ahmed, Amnesty International’s Senior Director for Regional Human Rights Impact. “Imaan and Hadi are being targeted solely because of their refusal to stop their fearless human rights work and for exercising their right to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.” The organisation also raised concernsthat the trial had been moved inside the prison, where Mazari and Chattha were kept behind a cage-like structure during hearings. The couple have faced several criminal cases in recent months. They have been in custody since 23 January, when they were arrested in a separate case involving an alleged altercation outside the Islamabad High Court. A day later, they were sentenced to up to 17 years in prison under Pakistan’s Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act over social media posts critical of the military. Pakistan’s Supreme Court suspended those sentences and granted them bail on 17 September – but they were arrested again the same day in connection with a separate case over a protest in March 2025, in which they were accused of chanting “anti-government slogans” and “blocking roads”. Mazari and Chattha are prominent human rights lawyers who have represented activists, journalists and marginalised communities subjected to enforced disappearances. Mazari’s mother, Shireen Mazari, is a former human rights minister who served in the government of former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan. The couple’s convictions have long drawn criticism from international human rights organisations, which have raised concerns about the treatment of lawyers and activists in Pakistan.

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : un plan sanitaire articulé autour de 16 piliers
items.description: Le Sénégal a mis en place un dispositif sanitaire articulé autour de 16 piliers pour prévenir et gérer les risques liés aux Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026. Le plan, testé à travers deux exercices de simulation en octobre, mobilise plusieurs structures sanitaires et forces de sécurité, a indiqué jeudi le ministre de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique, Ibrahima Sy. Coordonné par le Centre des opérations d’urgence sanitaire (COUS), en collaboration avec le Comité d’organisation des JOJ (COJOJ), le SAMU national, les forces de sécurité et les partenaires techniques et financiers, le dispositif prévoit des centres médicaux avancés dans les trois zones de compétition : Dakar, Diamniadio et Saly. Il comprend également une polyclinique au village olympique, un hôpital pédiatrique de référence à Diamniadio ainsi que des circuits d’évacuation sanitaire organisés avec le SAMU national. Le ministre s’exprimait lors d’une rencontre avec le directeur régional de l’Organisation mondiale de la santé (OMS) pour l’Afrique, le Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, en visite officielle au Sénégal pour accompagner les préparatifs sanitaires des JOJ Dakar 2026. Ibrahima Sy a précisé que le plan national avait été éprouvé lors d’un exercice de simulation sur table, le 15 octobre, puis d’un exercice grandeur nature, le 24 octobre, avec la participation de près de 180 personnes. « Les enseignements tirés ont permis d’apporter des mesures correctives au dispositif », a-t-il souligné. En parallèle, la surveillance épidémiologique est renforcée sur les sites de compétition, tandis que des contrôles sanitaires sont effectués à l’Aéroport international Blaise Diagne (AIBD), notamment dans un contexte marqué par les risques liés à Ebola et à la diphtérie. « Notre dispositif est en place, il a été testé et nous restons vigilants », a assuré le ministre, réaffirmant la volonté du Sénégal de garantir la sécurité sanitaire des premiers Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse organisés sur le continent africain. Il a salué l’appui de l’OMS et des partenaires techniques et financiers, estimant que les acquis de cette mobilisation pourraient contribuer durablement au renforcement du système de santé national. Les JOJ Dakar 2026 sont prévus du 31 octobre au 13 novembre.

items.title: Absa introduces instant loans for eligible salaried customers
items.description: Absa Bank Ghana is expanding access to personal loans with its Instant Loans solution, allowing eligible salaried customers to borrow up to GH¢350,000 through the Bank’s digital banking platforms. The solution makes borrowing more accessible by enabling eligible customers to receive pre-approved personal loan offers and access funds instantly through a fully digital process. Customers can check for available offers through the Absa Mobile App, Internet Banking, or an Absa ATM and complete the process without collateral, a guarantor, or a lengthy loan application. Director of Personal and Private Banking at Absa Bank Ghana, Charles Addo, said the solution forms part of the Bank’s efforts to make banking services more responsive to customers’ needs and expectations. “We are seeing increasing demand for banking solutions that fit seamlessly into customers’ daily lives. Instant Loans lets eligible salaried customers access credit quickly through channels they already use, while ensuring lending decisions remain guided by robust risk and affordability assessments. “This is part of our broader commitment to making banking more accessible, responsive and digitally enabled.” Through automated credit assessment, eligible customers receive tailored, pre-approved personal loan offers and, once they accept an offer, access the funds immediately. The solution is intended to support customers who require timely access to personal credit while maintaining the risk management standards that underpin the Bank’s lending activities. Absa Instant Loans forms part of the Bank’s broader digital banking offering, through which it continues to invest in solutions that improve convenience, accessibility and flexibility for customers managing their financial needs.

items.title: Badenoch condemns racist attacks after ‘Nigerian scammer’ remark
items.description: British Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has condemned what she described as racist attacks against her after a former aide to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called her a “Nigerian scammer”. Badenoch accused Reform UK politicians of exploiting her Nigerian background for political advantage, insisting that attempts to use her race against her would not succeed. She spoke during an interview on ITV’s Good Morning Britain on Thursday, following a series of social media posts by Raheem Kassam, a former senior aide to Farage. Kassam, who previously served as editor-in-chief of Breitbart News, described Badenoch as an “unrelenting scammer”. In another post, he wrote, “How are people still falling for this Nigerian scammer? Don’t give her your credit card number and bank account details!” Reacting to the comments, Badenoch said, “I think it just shows the sort of people they are.” “I think they think that maybe using my race is a way for them to improve their standing. “Britain is not a racist country, and because it’s not a racist country, their racist attacks and using my race as an attack form is not going to work,” she said. The controversy also drew attention to the response of Reform UK’s Treasury spokesman, Robert Jenrick, who declined to condemn Kassam’s comments. Asked during an ITV interview whether he considered the remarks racist, Jenrick said he did not, although he acknowledged that they could be unpleasant or rude. “It’s not my place to police everybody’s tweets who may or may not be a supporter of Reform,” he said. Farage had also faced questions over whether he considered Kassam’s comments racist during an appearance on BBC Breakfast earlier in the week. “I don’t think saying somebody grew up in Nigeria is racist,” he said. Following further questioning, Farage acknowledged that the comment was excessive but maintained that it was not deliberately racist. “Do I think the comment was over the top? Yes, I do. Do I think it was intentionally racist? No, I don’t,” he added. The post Badenoch condemns racist attacks after ‘Nigerian scammer’ remark appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 : la Fondation Wazni poursuit, pour la troisième année consécutive, l’accompagnement de dix jeunes filles
items.description: Conakry, 29 octobre 2026 – Dans le cadre du projet « Scolarisons 100 jeunes filles » , porté par la Fondation DiakaCamara, la Fondation Wazni accompagne depuis 2024 dix jeunes filles dans leur parcours scolaire et leur développement personnel. En s’associant à cette initiative, la Fondation Wazni a choisi de prendre en charge et de mentorer ces dix bénéficiaires, avec l’ambition de leur offrir les conditions nécessaires à leur réussite scolaire, à leur épanouissement et à la construction de leur avenir. À l’occasion de la rentrée scolaire 2026-2027, les dix bénéficiaires ont reçu, le 1er octobre à Conakry, leurs kits et équipements scolaires afin de débuter cette nouvelle année dans de bonnes conditions. Un accompagnement global La Fondation Wazni privilégie un accompagnement qui va au-delà de la prise en charge scolaire. Le dispositif comprend notamment la scolarité, les fournitures et les tenues scolaires, ainsi que des mesures destinées à faciliter le quotidien des bénéficiaires et à soutenir leur progression : goûter, transport, séances de révision et suivi régulier. Le programme intègre également des actions en faveur du développement personnel et de l’ouverture sur le monde professionnel, afin de permettre aux jeunes filles de découvrir de nouveaux environnements, de renforcer leurs compétences et de mieux se projeter dans leur avenir. Trois années de mentorat La poursuite de cet accompagnement en 2026-2027 marque une troisième année de mentorat auprès des dix jeunes filles. À travers un suivi régulier et personnalisé, la Fondation Wazni entend les accompagner dans leur progression, renforcer leur autonomie et les aider à construire leur projet d’avenir avec confiance. À travers sa participation au projet « Scolarisons 100 jeunes filles » , la Fondation Wazni réaffirme ainsi sa conviction que l’éducation constitue un levier essentiel d’émancipation, de développement personnel et d’accès aux opportunités. Céline Wazni, r eprésentante de la Fondation Wazni : « Investir dans l’éducation des jeunes filles, c’est investir dans leur potentiel et dans l’avenir de toute une génération. » À propos de la Fondation Wazni La Fondation Wazni œuvre en faveur de l’éducation et du développement social à travers des initiatives visant à améliorer les conditions d’apprentissage et à favoriser l’accès des jeunes aux opportunités. Son action s’inscrit autour de sa signature : Former – Construire – Transformer. L’article Rentrée scolaire 2026-2027 : la Fondation Wazni poursuit, pour la troisième année consécutive, l’accompagnement de dix jeunes filles est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Début d’une opération de rapatriement volontaire de 400 migrants sénégalais du Maroc, ce vendredi
items.description: Au moins 400 Sénégalais séjournant dans les centres d’accueil des migrants d’Argoub et de Bir-Gandouz, dans le sud marocain, vont regagner le Sénégal dans le cadre d’une opération de rapatriement volontaire prévue pour démarrer ce vendredi. “Une opération de retour volontaire des compatriotes candidats à l’émigration irrégulière actuellement accueillis dans les centres d’Argoub et de Bir-Gandouz au sud du Maroc se déroulera cette fin de semaine et la semaine prochaine. 400 personnes se sont inscrites sur les listes”, a indiqué l'APS qui cite une source diplomatique. Dix bus pouvant chacun convoyer 40 passagers vont ainsi partir du Maroc sur la base d’un programme planifié de concerts avec les autorités marocaines. C’est ainsi qu’un premier convoi de trois bus doit quitter le royaume chérifien ce vendredi. D’autres départs sont prévus le mardi 3 novembre et le jeudi 5 novembre tandis qu’une autre opération de rapatriement est en préparation pour la deuxième semaine du même mois. Trois pirogues transportant au moins 500 passagers, dont 300 Sénégalais, ont été interceptées dans les eaux territoriales marocaines par la Marine royale entre le 19 et le 25 octobre, a rapporté la même source. Elle signale la présence de nombreux femmes et enfants, y compris des bébés, parmi les candidats à l’émigration partis des côtes gambiennes et sénégalaises Une source diplomatique confirme que l’arrivée en nombre de migrants pose des problèmes d’accueil dans les centres du sud du Maroc où 800 personnes originaires principalement du Sénégal, de la Gambie, du Mali et le République de Guinée ont été recensés ces derniers jours. items.title: Rising utility bills wiping out workers’ pay gains – Minority
items.description: The Minority in Parliament says rising electricity and water bills are wiping out public sector workers’ salary gains. It is demanding an immediate review of the 2027 and 2028 pay agreement. The caucus argues that successive utility tariff increases have outpaced wage adjustments, leaving workers struggling to meet basic household expenses. In a statement issued on Friday, the Minority condemned the agreement finalised on October 28, 2026. The deal provides a 9% total remuneration increase for 2027, comprising 8% in base pay and 1% in conditions of service. It provides a further 10% increase for 2028. Mavis Nkansah Boadu, MP and Ranking Member of Parliament’s Committee on Employment, Labour Relations and Pensions, signed the statement. “Wage negotiations can no longer be conducted in a vacuum while utility regulators greenlight constant tariff increases that wipe out nominal pay adjustments,” the caucus said. According to the Minority, electricity tariffs have risen by roughly 29% since the start of 2025. It puts the cumulative wage adjustment over the same period at about 20%. The caucus cited three electricity tariff increases in 2025, which it said compounded to nearly 19%. Workers received a 10% wage adjustment that year. It said a further electricity tariff increase in January 2026, followed by a reduction in April and another increase in July, had deepened the pressure on household budgets. The statement also put the cumulative rise in water tariffs since the start of 2025 at roughly 18%. Beyond utilities, the Minority cited rent, transport, cooking gas and mobile data costs as further drains on workers’ earnings. It also questioned Organised Labour’s decision to accept the agreement and commit workers to a two-year framework. The caucus urged union members to demand details of the proposals their leaders submitted, the concessions they made and their reasons for accepting the deal. It called for the immediate reconvening of the Public Services Joint Standing Negotiating Committee to agree on a living wage that reflects rising utility and commodity prices. “We reject this insulting 9% pay deal in the face of relentless electricity tariff hikes,” the statement said.

items.title: Doctors Say a Rare Kind of Measles Is on the Rise
items.description: Each October, after the last of the tobacco has been harvested and the apple jam canned, Amish communities begin celebrating the months-long “wedding season.” Twice a week, hundreds of celebrants pack into a home to watch a young couple wed and share a meal. These gatherings, however joyful, add to the worries of Roberta Devers, a home-birth midwife in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania. At her prenatal appointments, she’s been asking mothers-to-be: With all of the celebrations, how are you going to keep yourself safe from measles? In Pennsylvania, at least 1,398 people have been infected with measles this year, according to recent estimates from the state health department; the Amish community, which has significantly lower vaccination rates than other Pennsylvanians, has been especially hard hit. Experts caution that the actual number of infections is likely much higher. “Every house that I go into, either my pregnant mama has it, her husband has it and she’s going to get it, or a family member has it,” Devers told me last week as she drove from one patient appointment to another through Lancaster County’s rolling farmland. Measles can be especially dangerous during pregnancy, leading to low birth weight, early labor, and miscarriage; one of Devers’s patients recently miscarried at 17 weeks while she was fighting a measles infection. If more pregnant women get measles, the number of newborns who have measles will almost certainly rise too. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics , historical reports suggest that about a quarter of children born to mothers who are sick with measles in the days leading up to labor will likely acquire the disease. No data on the current rate of measles acquired in utero, which is known as congenital measles, are publicly available yet. But health-care providers working in Pennsylvania say it’s on the rise—perhaps at a scale not seen in decades, if ever. Before the measles vaccine was licensed in 1963, roughly 95 percent of Americans contracted the disease in childhood, making them immune by the time they entered their reproductive years. But people who are of childbearing age today have lived through historically low measles rates. That means that a number of unvaccinated adults, including pregnant ones, never caught measles in childhood and are therefore not immune—and are now contracting the virus during large outbreaks. About two-thirds of the cases reported in Pennsylvania this year have been in adults ages 18 to 49, some of whom appear to be passing on the disease during childbirth. In an October 19 advisory , the Pennsylvania Department of Health noted that congenital measles had been identified in the state for the first time in decades. “It’s gone from something we never see to something that we are now commonly seeing,” John Goldman, an infectious-disease physician at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in Harrisburg, told me. The Atlantic ’s Tom Bartlett reported in August that an infant in Lancaster County, born to a mother who was severely ill with measles, was declared dead within 30 minutes after birth. [ Read: The measles-stricken mother who lost her newborn son ] Documenting an increase in congenital-measles cases is challenging. Case reports date back to at least the 1930s , but “no one has done any kind of systematic collection” of data, Adam J. Ratner, an infectious-disease pediatrician in New York, told me. The Pennsylvania Department of Health cannot release measles patients’ personal information, including their precise age, in order to protect their privacy, the deputy press secretary Stephanie Nojiri told me, and even if they could, no national definition for congenital measles exists to standardize tracking. Historically, doctors have diagnosed congenital measles when they observe a measles rash and other typical symptoms of the disease within the first 10 days of a newborn’s life. But that definition may unwittingly count some infants who contract measles in their first days of life outside the womb and miss counting infants with milder cases who do not present with a rash, Ratner said. Because congenital measles has historically been so rare, doctors know very little about its effects. Measles is known to wipe a person’s immune memory, making survivors highly susceptible to infections for years to follow; a 2019 study in children found that the virus demolished anywhere from 11 to 73 percent of antibodies and memory cells. And all people who contract measles are at risk of developing a rare but almost always fatal brain inflammation, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, that can occur a decade or more after they contract the disease. But newborns can react to viruses differently than children even a few months older, which could mean that the effects of congenital measles deviate. That dangerous brain inflammation, for example, appears to occur more commonly and more quickly in congenital cases than in cases acquired after birth. For now, doctors are trying to pool what they do know. Ratner, who is a member of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ committee on infectious diseases, helped assemble new AAP guidance on how to treat congenital measles; he and his colleagues consulted doctors in Canada, which saw congenital-measles cases during an outbreak last year, but also had to extrapolate from how pediatricians treat measles in older children. John Goldman told me that he and other physicians had been following that guidance, as well as the Pennsylvania Department of Health’s, and recommending both vitamin A, which can help limit the severity of an infection in children with a deficiency, and a dose of antibodies, which can help prevent an infected mother from transmitting the virus to her child at all. “There’s not a lot of good data on how you treat it,” Goldman said. But, he added, Pennsylvania may soon end up with the country’s largest data set of congenital-measles cases, which could help doctors treat those cases more effectively in future outbreaks. The best way to prevent a congenital-measles infection is, of course, to prevent a mother from getting measles before she gives birth. The best way to do that is with the measles vaccine, which is typically given shortly after a person’s first birthday. One of the few times an adult can’t get vaccinated is, crucially, during pregnancy—just when protection is most necessary. To help shield unvaccinated pregnant women, Roberta Devers argued that the providers who interact with them most often—in many cases, midwives—should be allowed to inoculate the other members of their household. In New York, Governor Kathy Hochul has allowed licensed midwives to administer the measles vaccine as part of a recent disaster declaration responding to the state’s growing outbreak. Pennsylvania, however, does not allow vaccines to be provided by traditional midwives, many of whom study through apprenticeships rather than attending nursing school and are not licensed by the state. Christian Macedonia, a maternal-fetal-medicine physician in Lancaster County, told me that’s for good reason: Providers who have not gone through formal medical training, he said, should not be distributing shots. But he also acknowledged that midwives are “really at the front line” of the congenital-measles crisis. In insular religious communities, such as the Amish one in Lancaster County, which have seen the largest measles outbreaks over the past couple of years, midwives may be the only medical professionals with whom families regularly interact. “We have intimate relationships with these families,” Devers said. “We want to be able to carry the vaccine, because our families started to request it.” Devers knows that many of her patients still distrust the formal health-care system. At a recent postpartum appointment, she talked with a mother who questioned the motives of pop-up vaccination clinics—she was suspicious of the shots being offered for free. As she spoke, the mother cradled her feverish 12-week-old baby, who had measles.

items.title: A Cynical Ploy to Block California’s Wealth Tax
items.description: The most important decision facing California voters this year is not which candidates to support for higher office, but whether to approve a wealth tax on the state’s approximately 250 billionaires. The ballot initiative that would impose the tax has plenty of enemies, among not only the superrich but also the many Californians, including Governor Gavin Newsom, who worry about losing the superrich to other states. But thanks to a deviously cynical electoral maneuver by the measure’s opponents, the people who ultimately doom it might include some of those who vote for it. Proposition 40 was spearheaded by Dave Regan, who leads California’s large and powerful health-care workers’ union, in response to the Medicaid cuts in Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. If approved, the initiative would create a onetime 5 percent tax on all billionaire wealth, and the proceeds—perhaps as much as $100 billion—would be earmarked mostly for state health-care spending. To make sure the superrich don’t flee before they can be taxed, the policy would apply retroactively to anyone who lived in the state at the start of 2026. Predictably, some of the billionaires in question are seeking to defeat the initiative. The Google co-founder Sergey Brin preemptively moved his residence and businesses to Nevada in 2025 and seeded the new political organization Building a Better California with $102 million from his stash. (That might sound like a lot, but the tax would have cost him about $12 billion.) Thanks to the donations of other tech tycoons, the group has raised more than $333 million in total. [ Read: If you tax them, will they leave? ] Plan A is to convince voters that Proposition 40 is unwise via a barrage of TV and social-media ads. In case that doesn’t work, the opponents have come up with Plans B and C: Propositions 41 and 42. These initiatives take advantage of a feature of California law: If two conflicting ballot measures pass in the same election, the one with more votes prevails. On the surface, both look innocuous and unrelated to the wealth tax. Proposition 41 is being pitched as a fiscal-responsibility measure, and Proposition 42 is ostensibly about protecting voters’ retirement savings. But the initiatives are designed to directly conflict with the wealth-tax measure. Proposition 41 would institute audit requirements for new special taxes and void any programs that are exempt from the state’s existing spending limit, which the new wealth tax would be. Proposition 42 would prohibit both retroactive taxes and any taxes on non-real-estate property, each of which describes Proposition 40. This tactic is completely legal, and efforts to change the rules could have unfortunate downstream consequences. For instance, if counterproposals were disallowed, then a group that caught wind of an upcoming initiative could block it simply by being the first to gather enough signatures. Still, the rule can, perversely, lead to antimajoritarian outcomes by preventing proposals supported by more than half of the population from becoming law if another proposal on the ballot happens to, or is designed to, negate it. Propositions 41 and 42 also take advantage of the possibility that voters will not realize that the measures conflict, and will vote yes on more than one of them. They might think that audits are sensible and that spending limits should be observed, or that personal property such as cars and engagement rings and 401(k)s shouldn’t be taxed, and fail to understand that these principles stand in the way of their belief that billionaires ought to pay a wealth tax. Other voters might prefer audits to a wealth tax even though they’d be perfectly fine with both; in that sense, the countermeasure forces them to choose between two policies that could coexist. Still other voters are likely to be overwhelmed or annoyed by having to parse so many measures and decide to oppose all of them: Political scientists have found that the longer the ballot, the more likely people are to vote no. [ Read: The one tax the rich can’t escape ] Historically, Californians are not easily fooled by this type of gamesmanship. But in a close contest, only a small subset of voters needs to fit into the above categories for the countermeasure strategy to work. Imagine that 51 percent of voters want a wealth tax and 49 percent oppose it. If all of those who oppose it vote for Proposition 41, knowing that the measure will negate Proposition 40, and just 3 percent of the electorate votes for both, then Proposition 41 will pass with 52 percent of the vote, nullifying the wealth tax that 51 percent of Californians voted to approve. Polls indicate that this outcome is possible. A September survey by the Public Policy Institute of California had the wealth tax passing 52–46, Proposition 41 passing 51–44, and Proposition 42 passing 54–43, which would result in only Proposition 42 (the one about taxing property) going into effect. (A more recent poll by the same organization showed the wealth tax at only 46 percent support.) A poll from UC Berkeley found that a larger slice of the electorate was undecided about the countermeasures than about Proposition 40, suggesting that some voters don’t realize the measures conflict. At the turn of the 20th century, many western-state legislatures were captured by the owners of local railroad and mining monopolies. Progressives and populists introduced ballot measures as a way to circumvent those plutocrats and return power to the people. But, as the fight over Proposition 40 shows, that works only if voters can withstand plutocrats’ efforts to capture the ballot-measure process too.

items.title: The Real Threat of Election Interference
items.description: I n a speech to the nation in July, Donald Trump said that reports from intelligence agencies showed that American elections were profoundly vulnerable to foreign interference. China had “bought, stolen, or hacked” voter data in 18 states, he said, and he implied that foreign operatives had somehow been able to manipulate actual votes. Reports by the CIA and other agencies that he made public that day did not back up his most extravagant claims. But Trump suggested that a foreign government may have stolen the 2020 election from him, and that it could strike again. Democrats consider that speech a dress rehearsal for next week’s elections. For years, Trump has claimed that foreign governments possess the power to hack electronic voting machines to change the outcome of a race. Election-security experts and lawmakers told me that they expect him to trot out the same claims again if Republicans lose large numbers of seats in the House and Senate. And they’re concerned that he’ll use classified intelligence reports as a pretext for trying to seize ballots or stop vote-counting by the states. “We start with the premise that the president is going to do that,” Representative Jim Himes of Connecticut, the senior Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, told reporters last week. But according to the most recent intelligence that Himes said he had seen about foreign threats to the election, U.S. adversaries haven’t changed votes. “We have never seen an operation to actually interfere,” he said. Years of reporting from intelligence agencies and election-monitoring groups backs Himes up. Foreign governments disseminate propaganda and try to undermine confidence in the political process, and they seek to influence policy, sometimes through espionage. But there is a big difference between influence and interference, which experts define as manipulation of an election with the aim of altering the outcome. Top Trump officials have sought to prove that foreign actors worked with Democrats and other “deep state” interests to deny Trump a second term in 2020, only for their theories to come up empty. Former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard went so far as to obtain voting machines from Puerto Rico and test them for evidence of tampering. Her probe found none . One reason voting machines are so secure is that they’re not connected to the internet. “It would be extremely hard for a foreign or outside actor to reach the actual vote,” Lawrence Norden, the vice president of the Elections and Government Program at the Brennan Center, told me. “And we have a paper backup of almost every vote that is cast in the United States at this point,” he added. So even if a hacker managed to flip a vote from one candidate to another on a computer tally, election officials could spot the discrepancy. Norden said that, in his view, foreign governments aren’t the major concern this season. Instead, the dominant source of worry is closer to home. “The new threat in this election is the administration,” Norden said. R eal limits constrain Trump’s ability to interfere in the midterms, even if he tries to do so. The Constitution gives states the power to administer elections, and U.S. law prevents a president from carrying out what many experts consider a nightmare scenario of “nationalizing” the vote. “A mere declaration by the president is not going to be enough legally to justify going in and trying to seize voting machines or ballots,” Richard Pildes, a professor at NYU School of Law, told me. Federal agents would need a warrant to take control of election equipment or ballots, and first they’d need to persuade a judge there was probable cause that a crime had occurred. Any classified intelligence reports might have to be shown to a judge, Pildes said. Even if the government was successful, it cannot legally remove the ballots themselves from state custody, and must rely on copies or images of them, he added. “There’s certainly no power in the executive branch to take over or nationalize the election process,” Pildes said. A White House spokeswoman told me that Trump was focused on prosecuting election crimes, including voter fraud, and on strengthening election infrastructure. The Department of Homeland Security has offered physical security and cybersecurity services to states and localities. “The only ‘concerns’ about election security are being caused by radical Democrats refusing to enact basic election security measures, supported by the majority of Americans, including voter ID and citizenship verification to ensure only Americans are electing America’s leaders,” the spokeswoman, Laruen Biss, said in a statement. “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.” [ Read: Trump still hasn’t found what he’s looking for ] Should Trump claim that foreign operatives are changing votes, Himes and his counterpart on the Senate Intelligence Committee, Mark Warner of Virginia, told reporters they would call the president’s intelligence advisers and ask for the underlying facts. Himes said that he told CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, “When the president makes that announcement, you will answer your cellphone to give us information about what’s happening.” A spokesperson for Clayton’s office told me that since he was confirmed this summer, he “has made it clear” to the leadership of the House and Senate committees “that he is available to them 24/7 on any issue.” A CIA spokesperson told me, “Director Ratcliffe is responsive to CIA’s Oversight Committees and will continue to be available as appropriate.” Recently, House committee members met with career staff in Clayton’s office who monitor threats to election security. It’s a smaller group these days, after cuts by the administration, Himes said. “But we got a lot of confidence that they are doing their job, that if the president were to demand that they make something up, one way or another, we would learn about that,” he said. T he threat profile from U.S. adversaries this fall is similar to what it’s been before other major U.S. elections in recent years. Russia continues to spread misinformation aimed at undermining public confidence in the political system, voting machines, and Democrats in particular, according to lawmakers and election-security experts. In some cases, Moscow-aligned actors are making deepfake videos with the help of AI to spread false allegations of misconduct . China has focused more on local races and influencing specific policies, often by recruiting agents in the United States. (In May, a former mayor of a Los Angeles suburb pleaded guilty to acting as an illegal foreign agent, primarily by promoting Chinese propaganda.) As for the Iranians, who historically have tried to influence U.S. elections, they appear more focused this year on keeping gas prices high by disrupting traffic in the Strait of Hormuz. Foreign influence has been a prominent feature of American politics for a decade now, since Russia used propaganda and selectively leaked emails to divide voters and denigrate Trump’s 2016 opponent, Hillary Clinton. But true interference would be novel, alarming, and contradicted by U.S. intelligence agencies’ best estimates about what foreign adversaries actually hope to achieve. Norden said that both before the election and just after, Russian influence groups are likely to again sow divisions and political discord. One Russian propaganda group in particular, Storm-1516, was active in the 2024 election and could come on the scene again, he said. But peddling misinformation, however corrosive, is not the same thing as flipping votes. Meanwhile, Norden said, the Trump administration has laid the foundations to undermine the public’s confidence in the outcome of the election. That is its own kind of influence operation. [ From the October 2026 issue: The election deniers’ long game ] Intelligence officials seem aware of that particular risk. Back in July, when Trump tried to suggest that China might have had a hand in his loss, the declassified documents that the White House put on its website didn’t substantiate those claims. One CIA document that garnered significant attention from lawmakers and security experts contained a summary of China’s aggressive efforts to exert influence on American politics and economic policy. But it didn’t claim that China had ever interfered and changed votes. If any renewed claims of foreign interference by Trump next Tuesday, or in the days that follow, are to be believed, they will require the sort of evidence that he has so far been unable to supply.

items.title: Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3bn 'complex' security breach
items.description: Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a “complex attack” that hit around $6.3 billion in funds, with about half that amount frozen to prevent a massive theft. The company — the world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes — said investigations had “uncovered additional points of breach”, contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance wrote on X. The firm earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that “user funds are completely safe” but also saying it would “cover all losses.” The company confirmed on its X account for Latin America that “the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion.” That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform. Binance warned the figure “may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” It said around $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen. The 2023 Bybit heist was attributed at the time to a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor. Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said Thursday it had “high confidence” that the Binance hack was also orchestrated by TraderTraitor, citing “robust on and off-chain intelligence.” “Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists,” TRM said. TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group – which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for “The Interview,” a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Fund freeze At about 0900 GMT Friday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended”. “Deposits remain unaffected,” it said. The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer,” allowing the unauthorised party to access a “service container” and execute unauthorised withdrawal transactions. “We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete. But it said later that “subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach.” Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether — a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT — said his firm froze about $1.6 billion “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.” Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC. USDT and USDC are both “stablecoins” or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar. The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Crypto prices tumble For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform. The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins. Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly 5 per cent and nearly 6pc respectively on the news. BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10pc. The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. Binance has secure asset fund Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website. “It’s becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them,” said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company. “My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn’t cover a hack of meaningful size.” World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance’s Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen. Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties. Incident adds to string of crypto thefts The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability to hackers. Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system. Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident. Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation. In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.

items.title: Two Ghanaians, Kofi Boat and Pascal, face up to 20 years in prison over $100m romance fraud scheme
items.description: Two Ghanaian nationals have pleaded guilty to their roles in an international cybercrime syndicate that defrauded victims across the United States of more than $100 million through romance scams and business email compromise schemes. Isaac Oduro Boateng, popularly known as “Kofi Boat”, 37, and Inusah Ahmed, also known as “Pascal”, 41, were described by US prosecutors as “chairmen” of the criminal organisation, which was primarily based in Ghana. The two entered guilty pleas before US District Judge Arun Subramanian in the Southern District of New York. Boateng pleaded guilty on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while Ahmed entered his plea on October 27. Both admitted to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, an offence punishable by up to 20 years in prison. “These guilty pleas demonstrate that geographic borders will not shield those who exploit Americans from facing justice in our courts,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald said. “Isaac Oduro Boateng and Inusah Ahmed helped supervise an international criminal organisation that preyed on vulnerable Americans, exploiting their search for companionship and turning their trust into a means of stealing millions. Together with their coconspirators, they orchestrated a massive fraud that stole more than $100 million from victims across the country.” How the fraud scheme operated According to the indictment and public court filings, Boateng and Ahmed were members of a criminal organisation that targeted individuals and businesses across the United States through romance scams and business email compromise schemes. Many of the victims were vulnerable older men and women who were deceived into believing they were in online romantic relationships with people using fake identities created by members of the syndicate. After gaining their trust, the fraudsters persuaded victims to send money to the organisation or assist in laundering funds obtained from other victims. The syndicate also targeted businesses through business email compromise schemes, tricking them into transferring money. The proceeds were subsequently laundered to West Africa. Millions of dollars in victim losses Prosecutors said Boateng and Ahmed, described as “chairmen” of the conspiracy, played supervisory and management roles in its operations. Boateng is being held responsible for approximately $12.5 million in losses suffered by victims, while Ahmed is responsible for approximately $28.5 million. As part of their guilty pleas, Boateng agreed to pay restitution and forfeiture of $12,529,213.98, while Ahmed agreed to pay restitution and forfeiture of $28,574,002. Judge Subramanian had earlier sentenced another member of the syndicate, Derrick Van Yeboah, also known as “Van”, to 85 months in prison. Another alleged member, Patrick Kwame Asare, popularly known as “Borgar”, remains at large. Ghanaian agencies assisted in extradition US Attorney Jamie McDonald acknowledged the assistance of several Ghanaian and US agencies in the investigation and prosecution of the case. The agencies included the Ghana Attorney General’s Office and its International Cooperation Unit, the Economic and Organised Crime Office, the Ghana Police Service, the Cyber Security Authority, the Ghana Immigration Service, the National Intelligence Bureau and the Financial Intelligence Centre. Other agencies included the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Drug Enforcement Administration’s Sensitive Investigation Unit, US Customs and Border Protection, the US Department of Justice’s Office of International Affairs, the US Department of State and the FBI Legal Attaché Office in Accra. Their cooperation helped secure the extradition of Boateng and Ahmed to the United States on August 7, 2025. The case is being handled by the US Attorney’s Office Complex Frauds and Cybercrime Unit, with Assistant US Attorneys Kevin Mead and Mitzi Steiner leading the prosecution.

items.title: Netanyahu's bloc finishes ahead in Israel election, but well short of majority
items.description: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp finished ahead of the opposition but remained well short of a majority, final results from general election showed on Friday, setting the stage for tough coalition talks or potentially another vote. Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing and far-right parties won 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, with his Likud party remaining the largest faction with 27 seats. The opposition bloc, led by centrist Gadi Eisenkot, secured 48 seats. The results from the Central Elections Committee also cemented the emergence as potential kingmakers of the Arab party groupings Raam and the Joint List, with the two winning a combined 19 seats. The fragmented outcome sets the stage for difficult negotiations to form a government that could last weeks, with no single bloc able to reach the 61-seat threshold needed and the prospect of another election remaining if talks fail. The final tally came after Netanyahu’s camp spent Thursday amplifying unproven allegations that Arab-Israeli groups received foreign funding to influence the vote, accusations rejected by both Arab-majority lists and Qatar. Israel’s Shin Bet domestic security service said it was investigating suspected irregularities, but stressed the probe was not intended to “cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote in a democratic and lawful manner”. The electoral commission also sought to calm tensions, with its acting director general Dean Livne saying any suggestion of widespread issues was “entirely groundless”. Political earthquake The controversy centred on allegations that Raam received money from Qatar, the energy-rich Gulf powerbroker that has channels to Hamas, to finance vote-buying operations. “The Raamgate scandal is a political earthquake. Israel’s elections have been stolen!” Netanyahu’s Likud party alleged on Thursday. Raam leader Mansour Abbas denied any wrongdoing and welcomed an investigation, while the Joint List accused Netanyahu and his allies of conducting a “campaign of incitement” out of fear of Arab voters’ growing political influence. Government officials have so far provided no evidence to back the allegations. Opposition figures accused Netanyahu of attempting to undermine confidence in the results after failing to secure a governing majority. “He is trying to challenge the election results,” left-wing candidate Yair Golan said. Eisenkot said he was briefed by the Shin Bet and the election committee, adding it was “too early to understand what happened, and whether anything happened at all”. But he continued: “It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election.” Netanyahu himself has long been under the cloud of allegations related to Qatar after the arrests last year of two of his aides for allegedly receiving payments from the Gulf state. Qatar called the latest accusations “ridiculous and dangerous”. Kingmakers under pressure Yousef Jabareen, head of the Joint List, told AFP that he is willing to cooperate with the opposition to bring down Netanyahu but without joining it in a government. Netanyahu had tried during the voting to raise allegations of fraud, saying that Arab parties were caught with envelopes of cash, and Likud peddled the accusations throughout Thursday. Police said they arrested three suspects but the election commission called it an isolated local case.
